summary.text: The Challenger Deep is the deepest known point of Earth's seabed, at the southern end of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean.
It is a small slot-shaped dip made of three basins lined up west to east, separated by mounds 200 to 300 metres higher.
A 2021 study put its depth at 10,935 ± 6 m, and it is named after the British survey ships HMS Challenger and HMS Challenger II.

items.prompt: Tiny creatures with hard chalky shells have trouble growing at the bottom of the Challenger Deep. Why?

options.label: There is no sunlight to build shells
Calcium carbonate dissolves easily under that pressure
The water is too cold for shells to form

items.explain: Calcium carbonate is highly soluble in the pressurized water, so small hard-shelled organisms struggle at extreme depths.

items.prompt: Many marine biologists now doubt the 1960 report of a flatfish on the bottom. What do they suggest the crew actually saw?
items.explain: A sea cucumber is known to live at such depths and might be mistaken for a sole.

items.prompt: Where does the Challenger Deep get its name?

options.label: A prize for reaching the bottom

items.explain: It is named after HMS Challenger, whose 1872–1876 expedition first located it, and HMS Challenger II, which established its record depth.

items.prompt: As of July 2022, roughly how many people had been down to the Challenger Deep?
items.explain: There were 27 people who had descended to the Challenger Deep as of July 2022.

items.prompt: The seabed topography around the Challenger Deep is complex. What explains it?

options.label: The collapse of an old volcano
One tectonic plate sinking under another

items.explain: The topography above the Challenger Deep is explained by the subduction of tectonic plates.

items.prompt: In January 1960 the US Navy made the first descent to the Challenger Deep. What kind of craft did it use?

options.label: A diving bell on a cable

items.explain: The first descent by any vehicle was made with the bathyscaphe Trieste.
